patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v3] mm: bypass swap readahead for zswap

version_history.subject: [PATCH v3] mm: bypass swap readahead for zswap

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch bypasses swap readahead for zswap, an in-memory synchronous backend similar to zram. The current implementation of swap readahead can lead to pointless prefetching of pages, causing increased anon residency and page cache thrashing. By bypassing readahead for zswap, the patch aims to reduce this overhead and improve performance. Measurements show significant gains in build time, zswap-in/out rates, and reduced swap readahead hits. The patch reuses existing code and adds a new helper function to check if a swap entry is synchronous.

review_comments.author: Barry Song
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Barry Song questioned whether the performance gain from bypassing swap readahead for zswap is dependent on the page-cluster setting, suggesting testing with values 0 and 1 to confirm

Reviewer Barry Song expressed interest in knowing if similar performance gains would be observed when using specific configurations, and suggested adding a mention of the 'page-cluster' configuration to the changelog.

Gave Reviewed-by
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Alexandre,

I assume your configuration is as below?

/ # cat /proc/sys/vm/page-cluster
3
/ # cat /sys/kernel/mm/swap/vma_ra_enabled
true

I am curious whether setting `/proc/sys/vm/page-cluster` to either 0
or 1 would result in the same performance gain on a zswap-enabled
system?

---

The change makes sense to me. I am just curious whether setting those
configurations would result in the same performance gain.

Maybe you can mention the `page-cluster` configuration in the changelog
as well.

review_comments.author: Yosry Ahmed
review_comments.summary: The reviewer notes a potential benefit of readahead for compressed swap, citing Kairui's LPC presentation, but acknowledges that this is not currently the case and assumes any future improvements would also apply to zswap.
review_comments.raw_body:
No objection here, I am just thinking about Kairui's LPC presentation
about how compressed swap can (in theory at least) still benefit from
readahead: https://lpc.events/event/20/contributions/2421/attachments/2116/4689/Better%20Anon%20(Swap)%20Readahead%20(2).pdf.

Seems like a big portion of the fault cost is still outside of
decompression and can benefit from readahead, but that isn't the case
today. I assume any future improvements to readahead and re-enabling
for zram would also cover zswap?

review_comments.author: Alexandre Ghiti
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer noted that the patch does not handle the case where zswap is disabled, and requested a check to be added to ensure that swap readahead is bypassed only when zswap is enabled.

Reviewer Alexandre Ghiti agreed to align zswap with zram, following Kairui's work, but no specific technical issue or suggestion was made.

review_comments.author: Alexandre Ghiti
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer noted that the patch bypasses swap readahead for zswap, but questioned whether it's necessary to do so in all cases, as some systems may not have zswap enabled or may be disk-only.

The reviewer ran additional tests with a workload of kbuild -j16 in a 768M memcg, zswap only, and observed consistent performance gains from bypassing swap readahead for zswap, including reduced build time, zswap-in and zswap-out, and swap readahead pages. The reviewer also confirmed that the results were the same with page-cluster set to 0.

review_comments.author: Barry Song
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Barry Song noted that if a high-hit-rate readahead algorithm is developed, it may be necessary to map all readahead folios at the same time in do_swap_page() to avoid increasing total work for synchronous I/O.
review_comments.raw_body:
In that case, if we can develop an accurate readahead algorithm with a
high hit rate for readahead folios, we will probably also need to map
them at the same time, as proposed in [1]. For example, if we readahead
4 folios, we should map them all together in `do_swap_page()`.
Otherwise, the cost of future minor faults can still be comparable to
the decompression cost. Readahead alone would therefore increase the
total work, which can be quite significant for synchronous I/O.

[1] https://lore.kernel.org/linux-mm/CAGsJ_4xM=WnFO-OuwVude-DQ_UkaCi_zF_bXBP9Li5+ZPNy0VQ@mail.gmail.com/

Best Regards
Barry

review_comments.author: Barry Song
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Barry Song noted that setting page-cluster = 0 could resolve the issue without the patch, but is still pleased to see the auto-tuning patch.
review_comments.raw_body:
Thanks! This seems to be a strong indication that setting
`page-cluster = 0` can also resolve your problem, even without your
patch. :-)

But I'm still glad to see your auto-tuning patch!

Best Regards
Barry

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Nhat Pham noted that bypassing swap readahead for zswap may not be suitable when multiple tenants with different swap backends (compressed synchronous and async IO) coexist on the same host, potentially causing issues.

Reviewer Nhat Pham expressed concerns about doing synchronous readahead work in page fault, suggesting it feels wrong and may concentrate work of multiple pagefaults into a single pagefault. They proposed offloading readahead to an asynchronous worker as a potential solution.
review_comments.raw_body:
If every tenants use zswap, yes. But we have tenants with different
kinds of swap backend in the same host (some using compressed
synchronous swap backend, some async IO swap backend).

---

I think we need some smarter readahead work, for sure. I'm just not
quite sure what it'd look like in the end, though.

Doing synchronous readahead work in page fault feels wrong. I chatted
very briefly with Kairui about this. Kairui is trying to come up with
smarter readahead heuristics, but I don't know - even if it's 100%
hitrate, we're concentrating work of multiple pagefaults into a single
pagefault. That sounds off to me?

Crazy idea time - what if instead of skipping readahead for
zswap/zram, we offload it to asynchronous worker (only synchronously
loading the target page)? That'll cancel out the latency issue at
least...?

review_comments.author: Barry Song
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Barry Song noted that asynchronous wake-up latency is highly unpredictable and can be much longer than the time it takes to complete mapping and decompression work in do_swap_page(), which makes async zram readahead unreliable without hardware queues.
review_comments.raw_body:
I am quite sure I tried this 3 or 4 months ago, and the
performance was very poor. The problem is that async wake-up
latency is highly unpredictable. For example, do_swap_page()
can complete all the mapping and decompression work in less
than 10 us. However, if we queue the work to an async thread,
its wake-up latency alone could be much longer than 10 us.

Based on my results, async zram readahead only works if we have
hardware queues rather than relying on async threads.

Best Regards
Barry

review_comments.author: Barry Song
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Barry Song noted that the patch bypassing swap readahead for zswap might miss some folios in the readahead window that are actually in zswap, and vice versa, but suggested not handling this complexity at this point.
review_comments.raw_body:
Yep, I have no objection to this patch. As I replied to
Alexandre, I was just curious about what would happen if we
set `page-cluster` to 0.

I think Alexandre's autotuning patch looks good overall. We
just have a lot of corner cases to consider. For example, we
might miss zswap and trigger readahead, even though some
folios in the readahead window are actually in zswap. The
opposite could also happen.

However, I don't think we need to handle all this complexity
at this point.

Best Regards
Barry

review_comments.author: Yosry Ahmed
review_comments.summary: Gave Acked-by

review_comments.author: Kairui Song
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Kairui Song suggested bypassing swap readahead for zswap, but noted that a better readahead policy is needed to avoid increased unmapping costs. They proposed evaluating shadow as a stronger hint for readahead and implementing proactive aging or a similar approach.
review_comments.raw_body:
That's a really nice POC! We should do that IMO, maybe with better
support for (m)THP readahead too.

We first need a better readahead policy though, or else unmapping
these folios might cost even more.

For the readahead part I'm thinking about evaluating using shadow as a
stronger hint for readahead after MGLRU-FG which helps distribute the
folios based on frequencey more evenly among gens, also with a more
proactive aging (async aging, or maybe lru_gen_imbalanced as Barry
once suggested somewhere) so folios in the same gen with same freq
will be much more likely to be reused. Or something similiar to file
readahead's PG_readahead based readahead. Well more
experiments are needed first though.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 0/2] mm: fix two allocator races with zonelist and cpuset updates

version_history.subject: [PATCH 0/2] mm: fix two allocator races with zonelist and cpuset updates

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/2] mm/page_alloc: detect zonelist rebuilds from memory hot-add
series_items.patch_summary: This patch detects and handles zonelist rebuilds caused by memory hot-add, which can lead to spurious allocation failures for __GFP_THISNODE callers. The issue arises when onlining a zone's first block rewrites the zonelists in place, causing intermediate list changes that can be observed by concurrent allocations. To fix this, the patch gates sequence checks on CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTPLUG, which covers all configurations that rebuild zonelists after boot. This change addresses a race condition between build_all_zonelists and page allocation, ensuring correct behavior even in the presence of hot-add events.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/2] cgroup/cpuset: use mems_allowed_seq when checking a policy nodemask
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the Linux kernel's cgroup/cpuset code where a spurious numa placement miss can occur due to a race condition between cpuset updates and mempolicy rebinding. The issue arises when a task's mems_allowed is updated separately from its mempolicy, causing the allocator to compare an outdated mems_allowed with the new policy. To fix this, the patch introduces a retry mechanism that waits for mems_allowed_seq to stabilize before checking the nodemask intersection. This ensures that the allocator always sees the latest values of both mems_allowed and the task's policy.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses two races in the Linux kernel's memory allocator that can cause inconsistent views of state between CPUs. The first race occurs when a CPU is rebuilding its zonelist due to memory hot-add, and another CPU attempts to allocate memory from the same node before the rebuild is complete. The second race happens when a task's cpuset policy is updated concurrently with an allocation check, leading to spurious empty intersections and unnecessary relaxation of MPOL_BIND needs. The patches introduce retry mechanisms for zonelist updates and use the mems_allowed_seq counter to ensure consistent views in cpuset checks.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the selftests/mm/madvise.c file where sched_getcpu() can return a CPU number above the maximum allowed, causing sched_setaffinity() to fail. The fix is to dynamically allocate memory for the cpu_set_t mask using CPU_ALLOC(), rather than relying on a fixed-size mask.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v2 00/10] mm/madvise: refactor cold and pageout page table walks

version_history.subject: [PATCH v2 00/10] mm/madvise: refactor cold and pageout page table walks

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 01/10] mm/madvise: name the shared LRU PMD callback
series_items.patch_summary: This patch renames a shared LRU page-walk callback in the Linux kernel's mm/madvise module to better reflect its purpose and functionality. The callback, previously named after its PTE implementation, is now called madvise_lru_pmd_entry(). This change does not introduce any functional changes but improves code clarity by aligning the name with its registration as a PMD callback. The patch is part of a larger series of changes to the mm/madvise module.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 02/10] mm/madvise: factor shared LRU folio handling
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors shared LRU folio handling in the Linux kernel's mm/madvise module to reduce code duplication and improve maintainability. It extracts common filtering and LRU operation logic into helper functions, making it easier to manage page-table-specific control flow. The patch also renames a function parameter for consistency and removes redundant parentheses from a file pageout check. No functional changes are intended by this refactoring effort.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 03/10] mm/madvise: use the PMD softleaf validity helper
series_items.patch_summary: This patch replaces a custom check in the mm/madvise code with the pmd_is_valid_softleaf() helper function, which is a central definition of valid PMD softleaf entries. The change simplifies the code and ensures consistency with the kernel's internal definitions. No functional changes are intended by this patch.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 04/10] mm/madvise: factor the cold and pageout folio split
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the code in madvise_lru_pmd_entry() to extract a new function, madvise_lru_split_folio(), which splits a locked and referenced folio into two separate folios. The original function is simplified by calling this new function instead of duplicating the same sequence of operations. This change does not introduce any functional changes but improves code maintainability and reduces duplication.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 05/10] mm/madvise: factor huge-PMD folio processing
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the handling of huge PMD folios in the madvise_lru_pmd_entry function by moving the checks and filtering into a new function called madvise_lru_huge_pmd_folio. This function returns NULL if there is nothing to do, allowing the caller to split the PMD lock before proceeding. The MADV_COLD young-bit clearing has also been moved into a separate function called madvise_cold_pmd. No functional changes are intended by this patch.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 06/10] mm/madvise: separate huge PMDs from the PTE walk
series_items.patch_summary: This patch separates the handling of huge PMDs from the PTE walk in the madvise_lru_pmd_entry function. It introduces a new function, madvise_lru_huge_pmd(), which takes care of advising or splitting huge folios and reclaiming them when necessary. This change improves code organization and reduces complexity by separating concerns related to huge PMDs and PTE walks.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 07/10] mm/madvise: separate PTE-batch folio processing
series_items.patch_summary: This patch separates the processing of PTE batches in the madvise function into smaller, more manageable pieces. It moves the per-batch work into a new function called madvise_lru_pte_batch_locked(), which runs under the PTE lock and returns a folio that needs splitting locked and referenced. The lookup of the folio is moved to a separate function called madvise_lru_pte_folio(), and the clearing of young bits in the PTEs is moved to another new function called madvise_cold_ptes(). This patch does not introduce any functional changes, but rather reorganizes the code for better maintainability and efficiency.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 08/10] mm/madvise: separate the PTL-held PTE scan
series_items.patch_summary: This patch separates the PTE (Page Table Entry) scan into two functions: madvise_lru_pte_range_locked() and madvise_lru_pmd_entry(). The new function, madvise_lru_pte_range_locked(), runs entirely under the lock and stops either at a folio to split or at the reschedule point. This allows for more efficient handling of large-folio splits and periodic rescheduling. No functional changes are intended by this patch.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 09/10] mm/madvise: make cold and pageout PTE lock ownership explicit
series_items.patch_summary: This patch makes the ownership of PTE locks explicit in the madvise_lru_pte_range() function, which is responsible for handling page table entries. The previous implementation used a restart label and an out label to map and unmap the PTE table, making it difficult to determine where the lock was held. The patch moves the PTE path into madvise_lru_pte_range(), which takes the lock at the top of each pass and drops it before splitting or rescheduling. This change does not introduce any functional changes but improves code clarity and maintainability.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 10/10] mm/madvise: share cold and pageout walk setup
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the shared mmu_gather and page-walk sequence in madvise_cold() and madvise_pageout(). The common sequence is moved into a new function, madvise_lru_vma_range(), which takes a flag indicating whether to perform a pageout. This change simplifies the code and reduces duplication. No functional changes are intended by this patch.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series refactors the cold and pageout page table walks in the Linux kernel's mm/madvise module to improve maintainability, readability, and performance. The changes split the shared LRU PMD callback into separate functions for each part of the walk, making it easier to audit and understand the control flow. Additionally, the series introduces new helpers for MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT, simplifies the folio splitting process, and makes PTE lock ownership explicit.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/8] selftests/mm: add MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT contract tests
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds contract tests for the MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT hints in the Linux kernel's selftests/mm module. The tests cover basic behavior, including that MADV_COLD does not populate PTE holes or fault swapped pages back in, and neither hint can be applied to a locked VMA. The tests also verify the swapped-page test works correctly when swap is available. The patch introduces new files for the kselftest harness and a C file containing the test code.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/8] selftests/mm: check that MADV_PAGEOUT skips holes and swapped pages
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds two new test cases to the madvise selftest suite in Linux. The tests, 'pageout_skips_pte_hole' and 'pageout_skips_swapped_pte', verify that the MADV_PAGEOUT operation skips over holes in page tables and swapped-out pages, similar to how MADV_COLD operates. This ensures that MADV_PAGEOUT adheres to its contract and does not attempt to populate or fault-in such regions.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 3/8] selftests/mm: check MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT range handling
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series adds tests for the MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT range handling in the madvise(2) system call. The tests check various edge cases, including zero-length ranges, unaligned starts, and unmapped gaps within the range. The patches also include a fixup to address an issue with sched_getcpu() returning CPU numbers above 1024 on large systems.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 4/8] selftests/mm: check that MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT reject hugetlb
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a test to the selftests/mm suite to ensure that madvise(2) fails with EINVAL when attempting to apply MADV_COLD or MADV_PAGEOUT hints to hugetlb memory. The test creates a hugetlb mapping, sets one of its bytes, and then attempts to advise it with both hints, verifying that the calls fail as expected.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 5/8] selftests/mm: check that MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT preserve shared memory
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a self-test to verify that the MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT hints preserve shared memory, including dirty shared file pages, shared anonymous pages, and SHM_LOCK'd segments. The test checks that these hints do not cause the pages to be evicted or written back, but instead leave them resident. The test requires root privileges to confirm through /proc/kpageflags that a SHM_LOCK'd page is unevictable. The patch adds new functions to map shared memory and page out ranges until they are no longer mapped, and modifies existing functions to pin tasks to specific CPUs and drain LRU batches.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 6/8] selftests/mm: check MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT on partly advised THPs
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds self-tests to verify the behavior of MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT on transparent huge pages (THPs). It checks that a whole PMD-mapped THP is swapped intact, that pages outside the range stay resident after paging out a base page or half of a PMD- or PTE-mapped THP, and that MADV_COLD on half of either THP preserves its contents. The tests also verify that a partly advised THP is split before reclaim, or skipped, to prevent corruption. The patch includes new functions for reserving and mapping aligned memory ranges.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 7/8] selftests/mm: check MADV_PAGEOUT file permissions
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a test to the Linux kernel selftests suite to verify that the MADV_PAGEOUT functionality works correctly. Specifically, it checks that an owner of a read-only file can evict a clean page from the file, and that unauthorized callers cannot evict pages from shared files or private mappings. The test runs as an unprivileged user, even when started as root, to ensure that capabilities do not interfere with ownership. Additionally, the patch includes code to map temporary files with specific permissions and to drop privileges for the test.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 8/8] selftests/mm: check that unauthorized MADV_PAGEOUT skips large file folios
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series adds selftests to verify that unauthorized MADV_PAGEOUT operations skip large file folios when only a partial range is advised. The tests check that the pages of a PMD-sized shmem folio remain resident, both when mapped with PTEs and when mapped with PMDs.

patches_reviewed.patch_summary: The patch proposes to make free-space tiering promotion bypass configurable, but the discussion centers around whether a global switch is sufficient or if per-workload policy control would be more effective.

review_comments.author: Gregory Price
review_comments.summary: Gregory expressed concerns that a global switch is a poor solution and suggested that the problem may already be protected by memory policy if the user set MPOL_F_NUMA_BALANCING.

review_comments.author: Li Zhe
review_comments.summary: Zhe acknowledged Gregory's point but proposed that a per-workload policy control could be more reasonable and suggested exploring Yafang's RFC for BPF-based per-cgroup NUMA balancing mode selection.
review_comments.raw_body:
On 10/14/26 9:16 PM, Gregory Price wrote:
> On Wed, Oct 14, 2026 at 05:43:45PM +0800, Li Zhe wrote:
>> Memory tiering normally promotes any recently accessed slow-tier page if
>> the target fast-tier node has enough free space. This preserves the
>> existing policy of filling available fast memory before relying on
>> hotness and rate-limit control.
>>
>> That is not always the desired policy. Some workloads may intentionally
>> place memory across CXL-attached memory and DRAM to use aggregate memory
>> bandwidth. With the free-space bypass, cold one-shot accesses and bursts
>> of hot accesses can refill the fast tier and pull the workload away from
>> that distribution whenever DRAM has free space.
>>
>> Add kernel.numa_balancing_promote_free_space_bypass. It defaults to 1,
>> preserving the existing behavior. When cleared, enough free space in the
>> target fast-tier node no longer bypasses the normal hotness and
>> rate-limit controls.
>>
> A global switch for this is a poor solution for this problem.
>
> Also, if the memory was spread out intentionally, it presumably was done
> so with a memory policy.  In that case, if the user did not set
> MPOL_F_NUMA_BALANCING - that spread is already protected because the
> mempolicy overrides the numa balancing fault and no migration occurs.
>
> I don't think this is the right direction.

I agree that a workload which wants to fully preserve its initial spread
can avoid MPOL_F_NUMA_BALANCING.

The case I had in mind is different: the workload wants to opt in to
tiering, so hot and cold pages can still be adjusted, while keeping the
DRAM/CXL distribution meaningful. This is the same kind of use case I
was trying to describe for weighted interleave plus NUMA balancing:

https://lore.kernel.org/all/20260930072617.64665-1-lizhe.67@bytedance.com/

With the current free-space bypass, opting in to tiering can promote
recently accessed slow-tier pages without the normal hotness and
rate-limit checks whenever the top tier has enough free space. That makes
it hard to combine weighted or interleaved placement with tiering
feedback.

That said, I see your point that a global switch is coarse. Maybe this
should be controlled by a per-workload policy instead. For example,
Yafang's RFC for BPF-based per-cgroup NUMA balancing mode selection seems
related:

Re: [PATCH 1/6] sched/numa: clear fault locality state on execve
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: The patch proposes to make free-space tiering promotion bypass configurable, but the discussion centers around whether a global switch is sufficient or if per-workload policy control would be more effective.

review_comments.author: Gregory Price
review_comments.summary: Gregory expressed concerns that a global switch is a poor solution and suggested that the problem may already be protected by memory policy if the user set MPOL_F_NUMA_BALANCING.

review_comments.author: Li Zhe
review_comments.summary: Zhe acknowledged Gregory's point but proposed that a per-workload policy control could be more reasonable and suggested exploring Yafang's RFC for BPF-based per-cgroup NUMA balancing mode selection.
review_comments.raw_body:
On 10/14/26 9:16 PM, Gregory Price wrote:
> On Wed, Oct 14, 2026 at 05:43:45PM +0800, Li Zhe wrote:
>> Memory tiering normally promotes any recently accessed slow-tier page if
>> the target fast-tier node has enough free space. This preserves the
>> existing policy of filling available fast memory before relying on
>> hotness and rate-limit control.
>>
>> That is not always the desired policy. Some workloads may intentionally
>> place memory across CXL-attached memory and DRAM to use aggregate memory
>> bandwidth. With the free-space bypass, cold one-shot accesses and bursts
>> of hot accesses can refill the fast tier and pull the workload away from
>> that distribution whenever DRAM has free space.
>>
>> Add kernel.numa_balancing_promote_free_space_bypass. It defaults to 1,
>> preserving the existing behavior. When cleared, enough free space in the
>> target fast-tier node no longer bypasses the normal hotness and
>> rate-limit controls.
>>
> A global switch for this is a poor solution for this problem.
>
> Also, if the memory was spread out intentionally, it presumably was done
> so with a memory policy.  In that case, if the user did not set
> MPOL_F_NUMA_BALANCING - that spread is already protected because the
> mempolicy overrides the numa balancing fault and no migration occurs.
>
> I don't think this is the right direction.

I agree that a workload which wants to fully preserve its initial spread
can avoid MPOL_F_NUMA_BALANCING.

The case I had in mind is different: the workload wants to opt in to
tiering, so hot and cold pages can still be adjusted, while keeping the
DRAM/CXL distribution meaningful. This is the same kind of use case I
was trying to describe for weighted interleave plus NUMA balancing:

https://lore.kernel.org/all/20260930072617.64665-1-lizhe.67@bytedance.com/

With the current free-space bypass, opting in to tiering can promote
recently accessed slow-tier pages without the normal hotness and
rate-limit checks whenever the top tier has enough free space. That makes
it hard to combine weighted or interleaved placement with tiering
feedback.

That said, I see your point that a global switch is coarse. Maybe this
should be controlled by a per-workload policy instead. For example,
Yafang's RFC for BPF-based per-cgroup NUMA balancing mode selection seems
related:

https://lore.kernel.org/lkml/3eda489898ebf7c848ce61760af745d9@kernel.org/

Would a per-cgroup control for this promotion behavior be a more
reasonable direction than a global sysctl?

Thanks,
Zhe

>
> ~Gregory

version_history.subject: [PATCH] f2fs: opt in to multigrain timestamps

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch adds support for multigrain timestamps to the f2fs file system by setting FS_MGTIME on f2fs_fs_type and making changes to handle ACLs correctly.

review_comments.author: Chao Yu
review_comments.summary: Provided a Reviewed-by tag without any technical comments or suggestions.
review_comments.raw_body:
On 10/12/26 23:46, Jeff Layton wrote:
> Set FS_MGTIME on f2fs_fs_type.
> 
> f2fs meets the multigrain requirements:
> - ctime updates use inode_set_ctime_current()
> - f2fs_getattr() calls generic_fillattr()
> - f2fs_setattr() calls setattr_copy()
> - s_time_gran is 1ns
> 
> Exception: with CONFIG_F2FS_FS_POSIX_ACL, f2fs_setattr() uses a local
> __setattr_copy() that sets timestamps directly, bypassing
> setattr_copy_mgtime(). Make it call setattr_copy() with ATTR_MODE
> cleared, then do the f2fs mode/ACL handling as before. ACL builds now
> also honor ATTR_CTIME_SET via inode_set_ctime_deleg(), as non-ACL
> builds already do.
> 
> Assisted-by: LLM
> Signed-off-by: Jeff Layton <jlayton@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Chao Yu <chao@kernel.org>

Thanks,

Re: [PATCH v2 5/7] nfsd: keep polling a layout recall answered with NFS4ERR_OLD_STATEID
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: The patch aims to prevent an endless cycle of CB_LAYOUTRECALL requests when a client returns NFS4ERR_OLD_STATEID.

review_comments.author: Jeff Layton
review_comments.summary: Identified a potential issue with an endless cycle of CB_LAYOUTRECALL requests when a client returns NFS4ERR_OLD_STATEID. Suggested squashing patches 5 and 6 together to resolve the issue.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Wed, 2026-10-14 at 07:06 -0400, Jeff Layton wrote:
> On Wed, 2026-10-14 at 16:30 +0900, Daejun Park via B4 Relay wrote:
> > From: Daejun Park <daejun7.park@samsung.com>
> > 
> > When a client answers CB_LAYOUTRECALL with NFS4_OK and still holds
> > layouts, nfsd4_cb_layout_done() sends the callback again after 10 ms to
> > see if the client is done. The repeat carries the stateid of the first
> > callback, although RFC 8881 section 12.5.3 has the server increment the
> > seqid in each CB_LAYOUTRECALL request.
> > 
> > The same section makes the seqid of a processed CB_LAYOUTRECALL the
> > current seqid of the client. Since commit dce72920c81b ("NFSv4.1: if
> > referring calls are complete, trust the stateid argument"), which is in
> > v6.8, the Linux client answers a recall whose seqid is not newer than
> > its own with NFS4ERR_OLD_STATEID, unless a LAYOUTRETURN is on the wire
> > (NFS4ERR_DELAY) or the layouts are gone (NFS4ERR_NOMATCHING_LAYOUT).
> > Before that commit it answered a repeat of the recall it was working
> > on with NFS4_OK until its LAYOUTRETURN was prepared, and with
> > NFS4ERR_OLD_STATEID from then until nfsd had processed the LAYOUTRETURN
> > (read from the code, not run). So a client from v6.8 on that needs
> > more than 10 ms to finish its I/O and to send LAYOUTRETURN answers the
> > second callback with NFS4ERR_OLD_STATEID, and an older client can
> > answer a later one that way.
> > 
> 
> What eventually breaks this cycle? The client has a newer layout, so it
> returns NFS4ERR_OLD_STATEID to the CB_LAYOUTRECALL, and now the server
> is going to continually retransmit that request. What makes the server
> eventually give up?
> 
> Or am I misunderstanding what causes this?
> 
> 

Oh, I think I see. The next patch makes it retransmit the
CB_LAYOUTRECALL with a more up-to-date stateid. That should eventually
resolve itself, I think.

It would make sense to squash 5 and 6 together so we don't end up with
this endless cycle if this happens on a bisect.
-- 
Jeff Layton <jlayton@kernel.org>

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v1] mm: unqueue deferred split folios outside the lruvec lock

version_history.subject: [PATCH v1] mm: unqueue deferred split folios outside the lruvec lock

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel to unqueue deferred split folios outside of the lruvec lock, which is held during certain memory management operations. The change introduces a new function, folio_batch_unqueue_deferred_split(), that can be used in these paths to release the folios from the deferred split queue after the lruvec lock has been released but before they are uncharged. This helps reduce contention and shortens critical sections with IRQs disabled.

Re: memcg stats flushing (WAS "Re: [PATCH] fuse: disable default bdi strictlimiting")
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: This patch proposes splitting memory cgroup statistics into two separate trees: one for in-kernel usage and another for userspace-only stats. The goal is to reduce the overhead of flushing statistics by only updating the relevant tree, which would decrease contention between concurrent flushers. Additionally, it suggests using node counters for root readers instead of defaulting to BDI strictlimiting. This change aims to make non-ratelimited flushes cheap enough for all in-kernel readers and potentially eliminate the need for a ratelimiting variant.

review_comments.author: Yosry Ahmed
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Yosry Ahmed suggested that Joanne Koong's proposed optimization, which involves skipping unused stats during flushing, may not be effective due to prefetching and cacheline fetching patterns. He recommended conducting a simple experiment to measure the impact of this optimization before implementing it.

Reviewer Yosry Ahmed noted that splitting the stats into two rstat trees, one for in-kernel hot counters and another for userspace-only counters, may lead to update conflicts across multiple code paths.

Reviewer suggested that eliminating root flushes should be prioritized before exploring other optimizations, and noted that subtrees are expected to be significantly smaller than the entire tree.

Reviewer pointed out that only updated cgroups are on the update tree, not their ancestors, and suggested walking the per-subsystem list without holding the lock
review_comments.raw_body:
I didn't measure this before, but I did tree adding a bitmask to check
which stats have updates and that actually made flushing more expensive.
It could have been the case that hot stats were distributed enough that
all the cachelines were being fetched anyway and the bitmask was just
added overhead.

I think you should do a simple experiment first about how much flushing
gets faster if you skip the stats not used by the kernel. It may or may
not matter, depends on prefetching (conversely, I wonder if explicitly
prefetching the entire stats array on each CPU would help).

I think it would matter less if we manage to completely get rid of root
flushes (except for userspace stat reads).

---

We have to consider the update side of things as well. How many code
paths will need to update both trees? That could be a problem.

---

would check if we can eliminate root flushes first tbh, then check any
other potential optimizations on top. Subtrees should me a lot smaller
than the entire tree.

---

Only the updated cgroups are on the update tree, not their ancestors,
not until the flush time. We used to put the ancestors on the tree on
the update side, but we don't anymore.

So we can only check the if the per-subsystem list is empty, not the
subtree specifically, right? Can we walk the per-subsystem list without
holding the lock or deleting first?
